author: Vipul Bajaj
title: How many of you have been in the middle of a fight and thought, I wish I could just show you the whole conversation. Not my screenshot. The  …
mainText: How many of you have been in the middle of a fight and thought, I wish I could just show you the whole conversation. Not my screenshot. The whole thing. I thought about that a lot. So I built it. A friend came to me after a fight with someone she cared about. She was certain she was right. She had the screenshots. She had replayed it enough times that her version felt like fact. I asked her to export the chat and drop it into something I had been quietly building. Twenty minutes later she went quiet. Not because she was wrong. Not because she was right either. Just because seeing the whole thing, every message, every gap, every time she reached out and every time she didn't, looked very different from inside the fight. That's ThreadLens. You upload a WhatsApp, Telegram, or iMessage export. Nothing leaves your browser. No account needed. You see who messages first, who waits longer, who says sorry more, who escalates. Patterns across the whole thread, not just the part you're angry about right now. There's an optional AI if you want to ask it something in your own words. It only sees what you ask about. It's free. I just think we'd argue less if we looked at the record before we loo …

author: Fei Peng
title: Build a compiler to solve Anthropic's interview challenge. Anthropic published their take-home interview challenge on Feb/2026: optimize a k …
mainText: Build a compiler to solve Anthropic's interview challenge. Anthropic published their take-home interview challenge on Feb/2026: optimize a kernel running on a simulated VLIW SIMD virtual machine to minimize cycle count for a tree traversal + hash computation workload. It has now been about 5 months since the challenge was released, so I am sharing my work as well. I hope this does not interfere with Anthropic’s interview process. The original intent of the challenge was for candidates to collaborate with an LLM and manually optimize the assembly program. I took a somewhat different approach: I built an optimizing compiler for the VLIW machine. The compiler can optimize not only the tree-traversal and hash program used in the interview challenge, but also the performance of arbitrary programs targeting this machine. My solution does not use any algorithm-level optimizations, nor does it contain any optimizations specifically tailored to this program or benchmark. Every optimization is a general-purpose compiler optimization. Result: CYCLES: 1137 Speedup over baseline: 129.9x Check it out if you are interested in techniques: Loop unrolling; Common subexpression elimination; Dead code …

author: Prateek Chandra J.
title: Quant Research / Quant Trading / Applied Science / ML Quant interviews are an enigma. You read the green book. You grind fifty challenging p …
mainText: Quant Research / Quant Trading / Applied Science / ML Quant interviews are an enigma. You read the green book. You grind fifty challenging probability problems. You memorize the birthday problem, the gambler's ruin, Monty Hall. And then you sit down at a Jane Street or HRT or Citadel and they hit you with a trading game, expected value games etc. you've never seen before and none of your memorized answers help. The problem isn't a lack of puzzles. It's that puzzles can come from any angle. The attack vectors are so varied that even after months of prep, you can stare at a problem and have no idea which path to take. Should you condition on the first step? Set up a recurrence? Look for a martingale? Draw a geometric region? The answer is always "obvious" in hindsight but finding it under pressure in real time is a completely different skill. That's the gap I tried to close. I wrote a long form blog post w/ Claude Opus that doesn't just teach puzzles, it teaches you how to recognize which technique a problem is asking for before you've solved it. 13 techniques. 30+ worked problems. A recognition flowchart at the end for pattern matching new problems on sight. This weekend, sit down w …

title: Cool tool. I got obsessed with the same question pretty early on Claude Code: where do the tokens actually go. So I wrote myself a small aud …
mainText: Cool tool. I got obsessed with the same question pretty early on Claude Code: where do the tokens actually go. So I wrote myself a small audit skill that digs through my own session logs locally and shows where the budget leaks. It tags every finding with a quality risk, so I don't end up saving tokens at the cost of worse answers. Ran it on two weeks of my data, found around 28% I could cut. Funny part: the command output that rtk compresses was under 1% for me. Pocket change. Almost all the money sat one floor up, in bloated context. Long sessions that cross 200k and drop into the 2x pricing tier, plus a pile of skills and plugins riding along in every request that I never once called. So compressing output helps, no argument there. For me the real win was just context hygiene. Different layers really, and they stack fine. Saving the tool, thanks for the pointer. … more

title: We’re excited to share the 2nd edition of QuantBook, a compilation of ideas from the world of quantitative finance by the team at Quant Club …
mainText: We’re excited to share the 2nd edition of QuantBook, a compilation of ideas from the world of quantitative finance by the team at Quant Club, IIT Kharagpur. The book explores a range of topics across five parts, from intuitive quant like behavioral finance, to applied models such as portfolio optimization, and deeper ideas in mathematical and stochastic finance. Along the way, we’ve tried to go beyond standard explanations, revisiting these ideas through careful study, clearer intuition, and in some cases small twists or extensions to the usual implementations. Our aim is simple: make niche quant concepts more accessible and spark curiosity for the field. #QuantFinance #FinancialEngineering #AlgorithmicTrading #MachineLearning #QuantClub #IITKharagpur QuantBook · 91 pages

author: Sid Chandra
title: Usually it takes 70-80 ounces of silver to buy 1 ounce of gold This relationship is known as the gold-silver ratio And throughout history th …
mainText: Usually it takes 70-80 ounces of silver to buy 1 ounce of gold This relationship is known as the gold-silver ratio And throughout history the ratio has averaged roughly 73 But markets rarely stay near equilibrium. As part of an ongoing series of small quantitative studies on commodity markets, I examined how the ratio behaves after statistically significant deviations from its long-run mean. Using daily futures data, the analysis focused on: • the historical distribution of the gold–silver ratio • deviation thresholds defined by standard deviation bands • the persistence of extreme dislocations • forward silver returns following these events Some observations from the study: • The long-run mean sits near 73 with a standard deviation around 14. • The current ratio lies close to the 20th percentile of historical observations. • Extreme deviations tend to persist longer than simple mean-reversion assumptions suggest. • When the ratio exceeds +1σ, silver has historically produced stronger returns over the following 30–90 trading day horizons.
